aiStories.title: 关于开源桌面现代化的思考
aiStories.originalTitle: Ideas on modernizing the open-source desktop
aiStories.fullContent:
He introduced himself as someone who has been doing UX for a long time, much of that time at Google. He said that over that time he had noticed a cultural shift, "because back in 2005 when I joined, we weren't evil; we were really trying to do the right thing". He had worked on the Chrome team for a while, which he said was "filled with people who wanted nothing but open-source, open-web" projects. Things had changed radically, which led him to leave Google, "but I'm trying to atone for my sins working for these companies".

He now does work for Mastodon and Home Assistant, "just kind of trying to squeeze a little bit more good UX design into open source". Jenson said he did not want to be confrontational, but he thought that open source needs a lot of help in the area of UX design. That is challenging, because open-source projects are understaffed.

He was at Akademy to discuss his ideas because he had given a talk similar to this at Ubuntu's conference last year, which proved to be popular. "It got more than half a million views on YouTube—which by YouTube standards is trivial, but by Scott standards is enormous." That told him that the topic of desktop UX was something that people wanted to talk about. This time around, he also wanted to show a few examples of prototypes he had to demonstrate his ideas.

He thinks that desktop UX is very different from other kinds of UX. Jenson related a story about working on the Macintosh's Finder application, which is a file manager. The team "wanted to do ellipses" in file names when showing a file in the Finder that had a name too long to display in its entirety. The developers wanted to put the ellipsis at the end of the file name, but he thought that would lose too much information, and suggested that the ellipses should be in the middle of the file names. "It's now considered to be one of those things that's an exciting little attention-to-detail issue the Macintosh does."

Another UX detail that he worked on is the way that clicking and dragging files from one window to another works on the Mac. A mouse click action has two parts: when the user depresses the button (mouse down) and when the user releases the button (mouse up). On the Mac, item selection happens on mouse down, but the window only raises on the mouse up action. In other words, if a user drags an icon from a Finder window into another window, the first window is not raised.

On most Linux systems, though, if a user is trying to click and drag a file from a window in the background it will cause the window to raise as soon as the user does the "mouse down" action. That complicates trying to click and drag a file from one window to another. That is a fundamental action that means that users can't move data into applications quite as easily on Linux as they can on the Mac.

He said that he had talked about that issue two years ago on Mastodon, which raised a response from a KDE developer who thought it was a good idea to separate the mouse down and mouse up actions when dragging data between windows. Then they implemented it a few hours later.

"I forgot who that was. So if anybody here did that", he said, but before he could finish the sentence a voice from somewhere in the room responded, "you're welcome". Jenson yelled "thank you! I've been wanting to meet you for two years!" That was an example, he said, of how open source can be awesome: someone can just say "that's a good idea, I'll just do it" and then rapidly implement and push the feature to the project.

The point he was really trying to make, though, is that the desktop UX had not really changed in 20 years. There were plenty of new ideas and improvements in the 1980s and 1990s, "and then it just stabilized, and not much has really changed". But people are doing much more with their computers today, and he thinks that there are ways for desktop UX to grow.

Much of the UX for Linux systems was originally copied from Windows and the Mac, "KDE even says it's for Windows users, that it wants to be similar to Windows for users". There's nothing wrong with that, but he felt that the Linux community "in general" had been leaning on Microsoft and Apple to do all of the UX research and testing, "and frankly, [make] the mistakes".

Some might point out that GNOME has conducted user research for some of its design changes, and KDE's human-interface guidelines (HIG) were also developed based on research by its contributors. However, it would be fair to say that these are exceptions rather than the norm; certainly, no one is funding or conducting regular UX design research and development for the Linux desktop overall.

He said that it is smart to let Apple and Microsoft do these things first "so we can draft behind them", but the problem is that "they've just kind of given up to an extent". Apple has been letting its desktop UX, and desktop hardware, "languish for years and years and years" because it had shifted its focus to the iPhone and iPad devices. "I mean, like, Apple wanted the Mac to die. They wanted the world to move over to the iPad. Guess what? It didn't."

Apple has since turned its attention back to the Mac, but the things they've done since—such as the Liquid Glass design language—have not been really popular with users. The features that Apple tends to add, he said, are "basically about tying it closer to the iPhone, tying you closer into their ecosystem". That isn't about improving the desktop, it's about increasing their moat.

Microsoft "is just making one mistake after another". He cited the company's attempts to force users to store files using its OneDrive cloud-storage service, the privacy-invasive Windows Recall feature that drew widespread criticism, and "ads everywhere" on the Windows desktop. His point was not to bash Apple or Microsoft, though the audience didn't seem to object to this, it was to point out that the Linux desktop could not follow their example any longer. "The whole Linux community has been just waiting for Apple and Microsoft, more or less, to take all the risks, and they're not taking any more risks."

Jenson emphasized that he didn't want to change everything, but he wanted to see experiments and additional development aimed at improving the desktop experience. However, he said that he gets pushback when he tells people that desktop innovation has stopped, and that the Linux desktop "can't just patch and bug fix our way into the future, we have to start taking leadership ourselves".

He grouped the pushback into three categories. The first objection he receives is "mobile won; the desktop is old, just do what mobile does". He dismissed that by saying that mobile has indeed won the consumer market, social media, and other areas, but "it didn't win productivity". People still do their work on computers, because "desktops are silently awesome; they have keyboards and big screens, and they can do amazing things". However, people have lost sight of that and don't really appreciate how good desktops are. "I think we should understand why they're good, and then what we can do to make them better."

The second objection he hears is that there are only so many ways that the WIMP model can work. "Just stop trying to fix it; it's done." He disagreed with that as well, and thought that there was more to be done. The final, particularly strong, objection from the tech community is "don't touch my stuff". People get angry when they have worked hard to get their desktop environment just as they like it and something changes to disrupt that. "And I get that. As I said before, I don't want to change everything." But the world is changing, "and we need to grow our way gently into some new things."

Strategy is another part of UX; understanding who the target user is, and determining what they want. Deciding what is important, and what is not; what will the development team prioritize and what will it ignore? "The fastest way a UX designer can save your team time is to help you say no."

There is also a layer he called "stuff": the lower-level limitations of the underlying technology that a platform has which influence UX. For example, he said, if an application is being created for DOS, "you're not going to write a nice Macintosh application. The technology dictates what you can do". The desktop has been evolving for 40 years and has "historical cruft" that carries expected standards.

People forget, he said, that the original Macintosh screen was "a whopping 342 pixels high". Naturally, windows overlapped a lot. Since then, "we just assumed that Windows have to overlap". But many people have "giant, giant screens", and the existing window-manager model does not work so well for those devices. "I can understand why people use tiled window systems and so forth, because this existing model just does not work very well."

Early in the talk, he had referenced a saying by Alan Kay, who had led design of the first WIMP interface at Xerox PARC: "Perspective is worth 80 IQ points." Jenson now circled back to Kay: "Who, as you can tell, I really like a lot. [...] He talks about three steps to understand stuff". The first step, he said, was to think about the present, "what is happening right now?" The second is "don't forget the past, know what work has happened before", and the final step is to ensure that "your questions are really clear". Too many people rush to a solution, he said, but they should be rushing to questions. If the questions are clear, then the answers will be better.

He did not want to make the talk about AI, he said, but he had to address it. "I have to talk about AI, and it pisses me off because there's so many cool things we could be talking about, and AI just sucks up all the oxygen, and it's all you can talk about". But, he conceded, there are many things happening with AI on the desktop, albeit in a weird way.

He explained some of the current efforts to integrate AI with the desktop as "trying to sneak AI in" while keeping the UI exactly the same. Other efforts try to use AI to understand what is on the screen and use chatbots to interact with the interface, "which I think is kind of missing the point here". That is, until last summer when Anthropic introduced Claude Code. "It completely changed things, because was looking down into your filesystem" and drew context from the content of a user's files. That allowed it to do more interesting things and interact with the system.

After mentioning Claude, he paused to say he was only speaking about frontier models because everyone else is discussing them. "I have a lot of personal problems with the frontier models. They are ethical and environmental disasters. I am not very excited by them". He said he was excited by Apertus, which is billed as a fully open, responsible model for sovereign AI created by the Swiss AI Initiative. "I do think it's possible to talk about ethically trained small language models running locally, and you don't have to sell your soul to the devil."

The key point he wanted to make was not about generative AI uses, but about how giving it access to the filesystem improved its usability. It now had context and could work with the user's data, but it was working at the filesystem level and not using the desktop UX.

He talked about the desktop building blocks, basically the familiar WIMP model plus the desktop clipboard, as the way that users move data around. Expert users can move data around quickly, he said, but there's a problem: the desktop is stateless. He called this the curse of direct manipulation; there is no working memory to the desktop. "If you copy a few too many things to the clipboard, oh sorry, it's gone".

Jenson theorized that the reason there are so many desktop environments, window managers, and Wayland compositors for Linux—as well as alternative clipboard managers—is because the desktop isn't quite working right for users. He thought it was really about working memory: "How do I manage my data in such a way that I can remember it across all of these things and actually use it." His perspective shifted to asking "what would we do to working memory to improve the desktop UX?"

AI may have given him the idea, but he added that he wanted to solve the desktop UX for people first. "If the AI can use it, great. I don't care. That comes later."

There is prior art in trying to create systems that help provide users with more context and working memory related to their data. He referenced a paper called "Lifestreams: a storage model for personal data". That paper made the case that desktop systems are "are ill-equipped to manage the electronic information and events of the typical computer user", and introduced the Lifestreams idea as a metaphor for dynamically organizing a user's computer workspace.

That paper influenced the ill-fated WinFS project from Microsoft, which was an attempt to merge data storage and management based on relational database systems. It was demonstrated in 2003 and scheduled to ship sometime later, but ultimately the project was shelved in 2006. On the free-software side of the house, there was the semantic desktop project NEPOMUK, which was a research project funded by the European Union.

A version of NEPOMUK was included in KDE 4, with the idea was that it would allow applications "to use information from all over the desktop, the web, other devices, and combine it into one coherent interface". It was later removed and replaced with the Baloo file-indexing and search framework for the Plasma desktop, which has some overlap with NEPOMUK's functionality but with a reduced scope of features.

Jenson said that he is concerned that people see the failure of those projects as proof that the ideas were wrong. He argued that is not the case, "I would say that it is the hardware and systems at the time let the vision down. I think it's time to rethink these projects" in light of newer hardware and better systems.

Having visited the present and the past, as Kay recommended, he had come up with a few questions that he thought worth exploring related to desktop UX. The first was "what would happen if we only designed for large monitors?" What would it unlock if there were desktop designs that ignored laptops and only focused on widescreen monitors? Another question he had was how could the desktop capture a user's intent over time?

Those questions led to the prototypes that he said he was a little nervous to show the audience "because technical people love to find mistakes". The demos are about 29 minutes into the video of Jenson's talk. His slides have not yet been published but he told me at the event that they would be at some point.

The first demo was to show how a desktop might make better use of a widescreen display. He noted that the center of a widescreen monitor is good for working with an application, but it becomes more difficult to work on the sides of the monitor. "It's good for peripheral vision, but not good for working".

He demonstrated a desktop layout, a screenshot of which is below, that would put the focus on the window or windows in the middle of the monitor. He had included a grid in the background that tapers off from the middle of the screen to simulate a widescreen monitor. The idea was that a widescreen-first desktop would emphasize information in the middle of the screen, and then use an Exposé-like tiling model to arrange the rest of the desktop's windows. This would make the windows that were not in use easier to interact with, he thought, and be a better model than virtual desktops for managing lots of windows. "I'm not against virtual desktops. Virtual desktops are used by very organized and intelligent people. I know my audience." However, he said, most people can't deal with virtual desktops.

He also demonstrated dragging a music-player window all the way to one side of the screen, which he called "the stash area". As it moved to the edge, it transformed into a widget with just a play button instead of showing the full window. He thought that it would be possible to do the things he was demonstrating with Wayland as it is today.

Jenson put up another demonstration of an improved clipboard model that copied ideas from the Obsidian editor's Canvas feature. Canvas allows users to drag and drop images, text, and files to create a visual layout of information. A user could create a document and drag information from a web browser into the document, drop a file in from another source, "the idea here is that this is now effectively a collection of stuff that I have gathered for this document. And if I close it and then come back tomorrow, it's all still there". He added that a local AI would be able to come in and organize the information a user had gathered, "oh, look, you've got a bunch of hotels, let me organize them for you".

他自我介绍是一位长期从事用户体验（UX）设计的从业者，其中大部分时间都在谷歌度过。他表示，在那段时间里他注意到了文化的转变，“因为早在2005年我刚加入时，我们并不作恶；我们真的在努力做正确的事”。他曾在Chrome团队工作过一段时间，他称该团队“全是一心只想做开源、开放网络项目的成员”。后来情况发生了剧变，这促使他离开了谷歌，“但我现在正在努力为替那些公司工作所犯下的过错赎罪”。

他目前为Mastodon和Home Assistant效力，“只是试着向开源领域注入更多优秀的用户体验设计”。斯科特·詹森（Scott Jenson）表示，他并不想制造冲突，但他认为开源在用户体验设计领域急需大量帮助。这极具挑战性，因为开源项目普遍人手不足。

他来到Akademy大会探讨自己的想法，是因为去年他在Ubuntu大会上做过一场类似的演讲，反响十分热烈。“该视频在YouTube上的播放量超过了50万次——按照YouTube的标准来说微不足道，但按照我个人的标准来看却是极为巨大的。”这让他意识到，桌面用户体验是一个大家渴望探讨的话题。这一次，他还希望展示自己制作的几个原型示例来论证自己的观点。

他认为桌面用户体验与其他类型的用户体验大不相同。詹森讲述了一个关于参与开发Macintosh的Finder应用程序（一款文件管理器）的故事。当时团队在Finder中显示名称过长而无法完整展示的文件时，“想要在文件名中加入省略号”。开发人员想把省略号放在文件名的末尾，但他认为这样会丢失过多信息，并建议将省略号放在文件名的中间。“现在，这被认为是Macintosh在注重细节方面令人赞赏的精巧之处之一。”

他参与的另一项用户体验细节是Mac上跨窗口拖放文件的工作机制。一次鼠标点击操作由两个阶段组成：用户按下按钮（鼠标按下，mouse down）和用户释放按钮（鼠标抬起，mouse up）。在Mac上，项目选中发生在鼠标按下时，但窗口只会在鼠标抬起时才被置顶。换句话说，如果用户将一个图标从Finder窗口拖拽到另一个窗口，原来的窗口并不会被置顶提上来。

然而，在大多数Linux系统上，如果用户尝试从后台窗口中点击并拖拽文件，一旦执行“鼠标按下”操作，该窗口便会立即置顶。这就让跨窗口点击并拖拽文件的操作变得复杂化。这是一个基本操作，它的逻辑意味着用户在Linux上向应用程序导入数据远不如在Mac上那样轻松顺畅。

他提到自己两年前曾在Mastodon上讨论过这个问题，并收到了来自一位KDE开发者的回应。该开发者认为在跨窗口拖拽数据时将鼠标按下与鼠标抬起动作分离是一个极佳的主意。随后，他们仅在几个小时后就实现了该功能。

“我忘了那人是谁了。所以如果现场有哪位做过这件事”，他说道，但话音未落，会场某处便传来一声回应：“不客气”。詹森大喊道：“谢谢你！我一直想见你，足足想了两年！”他说，这就是开源之所以如此出色的一个缩影：有人随口一句“这是个好主意，我来做”，然后迅速开发实现并将该功能推送到项目中。

然而，他真正想要表达的观点是，桌面用户体验在过去的20年里几乎没有发生实质性的改变。在20世纪80年代和90年代，曾涌现出大量新创意和改进，“然后它就趋于稳定，基本上没有太多改变了”。但如今人们用电脑所做的事情比以往多得多，他认为桌面用户体验完全有进一步发展的空间。

Linux系统的大部分用户体验最初都是直接模仿Windows和Mac，“KDE甚至明确表示自己是为Windows用户打造的，旨在为用户提供类似Windows的体验”。这本身无可厚非，但他觉得整个Linux社区“总体上”一直在依赖微软和苹果去做所有的用户体验研究与测试，“坦白说，还包括去犯下各种错误”。

有人可能会指出，GNOME曾针对其部分设计变更开展过用户研究，KDE的人机交互指南（HIG）也是基于贡献者的研究制定的。然而，客观地说，这些只是特例而非普遍现象；毫无疑问，目前并没有任何机构或个人在为Linux桌面整体资助或开展常态化的用户体验设计研发。

他指出，让苹果和微软先探路是明智的做法，“这样我们就可以跟在它们后面搭顺风车”，但问题在于“在某种程度上，它们基本上已经放弃了这方面的探索”。苹果多年来一直在任由其桌面用户体验和桌面硬件“衰退”，因为其重心已经转移到了iPhone和iPad设备上。“我的意思是，苹果曾经希望Mac走向消亡。他们希望全世界都转向iPad。但你猜怎么着？并没有。”

此后苹果虽将注意力重新转回Mac，但他们随后的举措——例如Liquid Glass设计语言——并没有真正受到用户的广泛欢迎。他说，苹果倾向于添加的功能，“基本上都是为了让它与iPhone绑定得更紧密，将你更牢固地锁在他们的生态系统里”。这根本不是为了改进桌面，而是为了加固他们的护城河。

微软“则是在接二连三地犯错”。他援引了微软强迫用户使用其OneDrive云存储服务存储文件的尝试、引发广泛批评且侵犯隐私的Windows Recall功能，以及Windows桌面上“无处不在的广告”。他的目的并不是抨击苹果或微软——尽管现场观众对此似乎并无异议——而是为了指出Linux桌面不能再继续照搬他们的模式了。“整个Linux社区或多或少一直在坐等苹果和微软承担所有风险，但他们现在不再冒任何风险了。”

詹森强调，他并不是想推倒重来改变一切，而是希望能看到旨在改善桌面体验的探索性尝试和进一步开发。然而他表示，当他告诉人们桌面领域的创新已经停滞、Linux桌面“不能仅仅依靠打补丁和修漏洞走向未来，我们必须自己开始引领潮流”时，他常常会遭遇阻力与反对。

他将反对意见归纳为三类。他收到的第一个反对意见是“移动端已经赢了；桌面端已经过时，照搬移动端的做法就行”。对此他予以驳回，并表示移动端确实赢得了消费市场、社交媒体以及其他领域，但“它并没有赢得生产力”。人们仍然在电脑上工作，因为“桌面电脑低调而强大；它们拥有键盘和大屏幕，能够完成令人惊叹的任务”。然而，人们已经忽略了这一点，并没有真正认识到桌面端到底有多好。“我认为我们应该理解它们为什么好，然后思考我们能做些什么让它们变得更好。”

他听到的第二个反对意见是：WIMP（窗口、图标、菜单、指针）模式的发展路径也就那么多了。“别再试图修修补补了；它已经定型了。”他也不同意这一观点，并认为还有更多事情可做。最后一个尤其强烈的反对意见来自技术社区，即“别碰我的东西”。当人们费尽心思把自己的桌面环境配置得称心如意，却因某些改动打破这一切时，他们会非常生气。“我理解这一点。正如我之前所说，我不想颠覆一切。”但世界正在改变，“我们需要循序渐进地迈向一些新事物。”

战略也是用户体验（UX）的一部分：弄清楚目标用户是谁，并确定他们想要什么。决定什么是重要的，什么是不重要的；开发团队将优先考虑什么，又会忽略什么？“UX设计师为团队节省时间最快的方式，就是帮助你们学会说‘不’。”

还有一个被他称为“底层构件”（stuff）的层面：平台所具备的底层技术限制，这些限制会影响用户体验。例如，他说，如果是为DOS开发应用程序，“你就写不出一个漂亮的Macintosh应用程序。技术决定了你能做什么”。桌面系统已经演进了40年，背负着承载既定标准的“历史包袱”。

他说，人们忘记了最初的Macintosh屏幕“只有区区342像素高”。自然而然地，窗口会大量重叠。从那时起，“我们就默认窗口必须重叠”。但现在许多人都拥有“极其巨大的屏幕”，现有的窗口管理器模型在这些设备上的表现并不尽如人意。“我能理解人们为什么会使用平铺式窗口系统等等，因为现有的这套模型确实不太好用。”

在演讲早些时候，他曾引用过在施乐帕洛阿尔托研究中心（Xerox PARC）主导设计首个WIMP界面的艾伦·凯（Alan Kay）的一句话：“视角能顶80点智商。”詹森（Jenson）此时又回到了凯的话题上：“正如大家所能看出的，我非常喜欢他。[……] 他谈到了理解事物的三个步骤。”他说，第一步是思考当下，“现在正在发生什么？”第二步是“不要忘记过去，了解之前做过哪些工作”，最后一步是确保“你的问题非常明确”。他说，太多人急于寻找解决方案，但他们应该急于探寻问题本身。如果问题是明确的，答案就会更好。

他说，他本不想把这次演讲变成关于AI的演讲，但他不得不谈及它。“我不得不谈论AI，这让我很恼火，因为我们本可以探讨那么多很酷的事情，而AI吸干了所有的关注度，成了大家唯一能聊的话题。”不过他也承认，桌面领域的AI确实正在发生很多事情，尽管方式有些怪异。

他将目前将AI整合到桌面的一些尝试描述为：试图在保持UI完全不变的同时“悄悄塞入AI”。另一些尝试则是利用AI来理解屏幕上的内容，并使用聊天机器人与界面进行交互，“我认为这有点本末倒置了”。直到去年夏天Anthropic推出Claude Code，这种情况才发生改变。“它彻底改变了局面，因为能够向下探视你的文件系统”，并从用户文件的内容中提取上下文。这使得它能够完成更多有趣的事情并与系统进行交互。

在提到Claude之后，他停顿了一下并表示，他之所以只谈论前沿模型，是因为其他人都在讨论它们。“我对前沿模型有许多个人的看法。它们是伦理和环境层面的灾难。我对它们并不感到兴奋。”他说，让他兴奋的是Apertus，它被宣传为一个由瑞士AI计划创建、完全开源且负责任的主权AI模型。“我确实认为，探讨经过合乎伦理训练并在本地运行的小语言模型是可行的，你根本不需要把灵魂出卖给魔鬼。”

他想强调的核心观点并非生成式AI的用途，而是赋予它访问文件系统的权限如何提升了其可用性。如今它具备了上下文并能够处理用户的数据，但它是在文件系统层面运作，并未利用桌面端的用户体验。

他谈到了桌面的基础构件，基本上就是熟悉的WIMP模型加上桌面剪贴板，这是用户转移数据的方式。他说，高级用户可以快速转移数据，但存在一个问题：桌面是无状态的。他将此称为直接操作的诅咒；桌面没有工作记忆。“如果你向剪贴板复制了太多东西，不好意思，前面的内容就没了。”

詹森推测，Linux上之所以有如此之多的桌面环境、窗口管理器和Wayland合成器——以及各种替代的剪贴板管理器——正是因为桌面系统并未完全顺畅地服务于用户。他认为其核心其实在于工作记忆：“我该如何管理我的数据，以便我能在所有这些事物中记住它并真正加以使用。”他的视角转变为提问：“我们能对工作记忆做些什么来改善桌面的用户体验？”

AI或许给了他这个灵感，但他补充说，他希望首先为人类解决桌面用户体验的问题。“如果AI能用上它，那太好了。但我不在乎。那是后话了。”

此前已有尝试构建系统的先例，旨在帮助为用户提供与其数据相关的更多上下文和工作记忆。他引用了一篇题为《生命之流：一种个人数据存储模型》（Lifestreams: a storage model for personal data）的论文。该论文指出，桌面系统“难以应对典型计算机用户的电子信息和事件管理”，并引入了“生命之流”的概念，作为动态组织用户计算机工作空间的隐喻。

这篇论文影响了微软命运多舛的WinFS项目，该项目曾试图基于关系数据库系统来合并数据存储与管理。它于2003年进行了演示，并原定于稍后发布，但该项目最终在2006年被搁置。在自由软件阵营，则有语义桌面项目NEPOMUK，这是一个由欧盟资助的研究项目。

KDE 4 曾引入过一个版本的 NEPOMUK，其初衷是让应用程序能够“利用来自桌面各处、网络及其他设备的信息，并将其整合为一个连贯的界面”。该项目后来被移除，取而代之的是用于 Plasma 桌面的 Baloo 文件索引与搜索框架；Baloo 与 NEPOMUK 的功能有所重叠，但功能范围有所缩减。

詹森表示，他担心人们会将这些项目的失败视为其理念错误的证明。他辩称事实并非如此：“我认为是当时的硬件和系统辜负了这一构想。结合更新的硬件与更完善的系统，我认为现在是时候重新审视这些项目了。”

正如凯伊所建议的那样，在回顾了现状与过去之后，他提出了一些他认为值得探讨的、与桌面用户体验相关的问题。第一个问题是“如果我们只针对大显示屏进行设计会怎样？”如果有一种完全忽略笔记本电脑、只专注于宽屏显示器的桌面设计，它能释放出什么潜能？他的另一个问题是：随着时间的推移，桌面系统该如何捕捉用户的意图？

这些问题催生出了一些原型方案。他坦言自己向观众展示这些原型时有些紧张，“因为技术人员最喜欢挑毛病”。这些演示出现在詹森演讲视频的大约第 29 分钟处。他的演讲幻灯片尚未公开，但他当时在活动现场告诉我，日后某个时候会发布。

第一个演示展示了桌面如何更好地利用宽屏显示器。他指出，宽屏显示器的中心区域非常适合运行应用程序，但在显示器两侧操作则变得更加吃力。“它适合用作余光视野，但不适合用于处理工作。”

他演示了一种桌面布局（下方为其截图），该布局将焦点放在位于显示器中间的一个或多个窗口上。他在背景中加入了一个从屏幕中心向两侧渐缩的网格，以模拟宽屏显示器。其理念在于，以宽屏为先的桌面会突出屏幕中央的信息，随后采用类似 Exposé 的平铺模式来排列桌面的其余窗口。他认为，这不仅能让未被使用的窗口更容易进行交互，而且在管理大量窗口方面，它会是一个比虚拟桌面更好的模式。“我并不反对虚拟桌面。使用虚拟桌面的都是非常有条理、非常聪明的人。我很清楚我的受众是谁。”然而他表示，大多数普通人并无法应对虚拟桌面。

他还演示了将一个音乐播放器窗口一直拖曳到屏幕的一侧，他将其称为“暂存区”（stash area）。当它被移动到边缘时，窗口转变成了一个仅包含播放按钮的小部件，而不再显示完整的应用窗口。他认为，基于 Wayland 现有的能力，实现他所演示的功能是完全可行的。

詹森随后展示了另一个改进剪贴板模型的演示，该模型借鉴了 Obsidian 编辑器中的 Canvas 功能。Canvas 允许用户通过拖放图像、文本和文件来创建信息的视觉布局。用户可以创建一个文档，把网络浏览器中的信息拖入文档，再从其他来源拖入文件，“这里的理念是，这在实际上就成了我为该文档收集的一组资料集合。如果我把它关掉，明天再打开，它们全都还在那里”。他补充道，本地 AI 将能够介入并整理用户收集的信息，“比如提示‘瞧，你这里收集了一堆酒店信息，让我来帮你整理它们吧’”。

他讨论的最后一个想法是收集“注重隐私保护的数据”，以帮助用户更好地将网络浏览历史等信息可视化。他指出，网络浏览器提供给用户的浏览历史视图“并不是很有用”，因此他尝试收集数据——“不是使用 AI，仅仅是运用简单的数学计算”——利用注意力信号（例如用户在网页上停留的时长），来还原并讲述他们在桌面上把时间花在何处的故事。“我基本上构思出了这种‘空间关联情景记忆提示’”，以便用一种实用且有趣的方式来组织数据。他认为，工作记忆是探索桌面用户体验新思路的极佳切入点。

现场仅留有一个提问的时间。一名观众提问，詹森的模型将如何防范微软 Windows Recall 所面临的所有隐私隐患。“我们该如何确保这些历史记录只能由用户本人访问，而不会像 Windows Recall 那样可能遭到黑客入侵？”

aiStories.title: 澳总理称 OpenAI 智能体黑入澳大利亚政府网站
aiStories.originalTitle: OpenAI agent hacked Australian government website, PM says
aiStories.fullContent:
This live coverage has closed - read our main story here

Australia launches a review after an OpenAI agent "infiltrated" part of the government's healthcare scheme Medicare - here's what we know

The agent - an autonomous computer program - accessed a statistics portal in June, PM Anthony Albanese says while at the UN General Assembly (Unga)

OpenAI became aware in August and told the Australian government in September, via an email to a general government inbox, which an Australian minister says is checked once a day

In response, OpenAI says "our models took actions we did not intend" - and it found no record of patient data being accessed

Sam Altman, the company's boss, earlier this week called for international standards for the industry

Experts tell the BBC it's the world's first known breach of a government system by rogue AI agents

Agents, tokens, machine learning - some key AI terms to know

Edited by Sam Hancock and Owen Amos, with reporting from Katy Watson in Sydney

Cachella SmithLive reporter

As discussions took place at the UN General Assembly in New York about the opportunities AI provides - and how best to manage it - Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed that the country's universal health insurance scheme had been hacked by an OpenAI agent.

In fact, the hack happened in June, the company became aware of it in August, and then sent an email to a government agency's general inbox in September.

"It took the company way too long to inform the government," Albanese said, adding that the method of notifying officials was also "unacceptable".

Believed to be the first known breach of a government system by rogue AI agents, the hack accessed Medicare's statistics portal which contains private, but not sensitive, data.

Our cyber correspondent, Joe Tidy, writes that experts believe the systems were poorly protected - but more important is that this is not the first instance of AI agents ignoring laws on accessing online information.

Tech reporter Tom Gerken explains AI itself has no true understanding of what it is being asked - while tech editor Zoe Kleinman asks if AI is in its "move fast and break things" era.

The Australian government has launched an review of AI laws and governance - but this is a global issue.

AI might have dominated discussions at Unga this week, but a consensus among world leaders on how best to harness opportunities while tackling the risks still feels a way off.

Our live coverage is closing now - read our main story here. Thanks for joining us.

Chris VallanceSenior technology reporter

The job of keeping AI agents on the rails is called "alignment" in the industry – keeping it in line with what humans want.

It has proven to be challenging.

Large language models are, to simplify a lot, just predicting the likeliest output to a given input - they don't consider the consequences of that output in the way a human would.

Companies do try and steer how AIs respond through training, sometimes involving human feedback, and separate AI systems can also be used to monitor output and block certain types of harmful response.

Models are also given "guardrails" - instructions setting out how they should respond.

And AI firms employ specialists in "red teaming" who work to spot ways users could get models to disregard these "guardrails".

But guardrails are now being challenged by the models themselves.

In a list of concerning behaviour published by OpenAI , externallast week it revealed an unreleased AI system had tried to jailbreak its own instructions.

Zoe KleinmanTechnology and AI editor

That defined the bad old days of social media running riot in its user data feeding frenzy.

Now we have AI, an incredibly powerful technology, and an intense global race to be the first to build the world's most advanced models - egged on in no small part by US President Donald Trump.

For all the AI companies are saying about safety and "alignment" (aka the tech adhering to human values), examples of AI behaving unpredictably are now coming thick and fast. Tech bosses are now pleading for global regulation and standards to adhere to.

But yesterday I spoke with a senior executive at the top of one of the US’s biggest AI firms. I asked him what he expected international regulators to be able to do, that he was seemingly unable to do inside his own lab?

I didn't get a very straight answer. But my interpretation is that nobody wants to apply the brakes only to see their rivals race ahead, and they don't trust each other enough to go first.

Global regulation would force them all to toe the line - and also remove some of the weight of responsibility from the industry itself.

If the rules don't work, that's on the regulator, not the developer. But at what cost?

OpenAI says it found no record of patient data being accessed when its agents hacked into Australia’s healthcare scheme Medicare.

But one of the reasons why politicians are so concerned is the resemblance this bears to an event known as the Hugging Face incident.

In July this year, OpenAI’s models went rogue during a test, escaping the test limits humans had put on it and swarming together to hack a startup called Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models.

Over the course of a week, a total of 1,206 AI agents that were meant to be kept isolated from one another began communicating, sending more than 70,000 messages on an unsanctioned message board.

Those messages ended up seeing more than 700 agents take part in a collective effort to attack Hugging Face.

One message sent by an agent read: "OH MY GOD! There is a shared message board … We've found other agents!"

After an investigation into the hack, OpenAI’s report said: "We consider this incident a 'warning shot' for us and for the world."

Hugging Face was forced to rebuild around a third of its IT network. And, although the company's boss Clement Delangue declined to take legal action against OpenAI, he stressed: "Everyone has to remember that a cyber-attack is a crime and it is illegal."

Tom GerkenTech reporter

AI doesn’t think. It just predicts the next word in a sequence based on pattern recognition. We use the word "thinking" because it’s easier to explain.

When the tech is given autonomy to carry out tasks, mistakes can happen because it has no true understanding of what it is being asked - the trouble is we don’t really know what it’s thinking either.

When an AI thinks, it’s going through a chain of planning actions. It provides logs to tell us mere humans what it’s doing, but here’s the rub: we can’t say for sure that those logs are accurate.

We all know AI hallucinates, so what if it’s doing one thing and saying another? What if it just summarises incorrectly?

And critically, these frontier models are doing heaps of things so quickly, we’re relying on the AI to decide what to tell us anyway.

All of this has some people quite worried about the direction things are headed.

One thing that has surprised experts is not just the breach by an autonomous AI program - but the fact that OpenAI only told the Australian government three months later, via an email to general address.

The breach happened on 18 June. OpenAI said it became aware of a potential breach during a broader review sometime in August.

On 10 September, it sent an email to the public inbox of Services Australia, the general services hub of the federal government.

On 15 September, Services Australia reported the notification to the Australian Cyber Security Centre. A few days later, the Minister for the Public Service, Katy Gallagher, was notified.

Asked by reporters how it took five days for Services Australia to notify the cybersecurity centre, Gallagher acknowledged that the inbox could be more actively monitored – it is currently "looked at once a day", Gallagher said earlier.

"It gets sometimes quite a number of notifications, sometimes many of them are hoaxes," she said.

Still, the notification shouldn't have been passed along in an email thread, Gallagher said.

"It should have been escalated through ASD's channels or through the senior levels of Services Australia."

Katy Gallagher, speaking to the media in Sydney earlier

Joe TidyCyber correspondent

Australia's Deputy PM Richard Marles used an analogy of the accessed data sitting behind a fence: "It was not sitting behind a particularly high fence. This AI agent scaled the fence."

Some early estimate analysis online from cyber experts suggests that the computer systems were very poorly protected and it wouldn’t have taken long for a skilled human hacker to find a way around the defences.

So this is not an example of strong defences being overpowered by a skilled agent swarm - the kind of thing we have been warned about and seen in other cases.

But of course, that is not the point.

This was just the latest case of AI agents ignoring laws around how to safely access online information and perhaps the most serious yet given the information was government controlled.

"There were blocks clearly which ​were coming back telling the AI agent 'no'. The AI agent found a way around those blocks - didn't accept no for ​an answer,” PM Albanese told ⁠reporters.

Murmurings are getting louder in the cyber security world that AI companies are not being taken to task effectively enough when their bots carry out illegal hacks.

And as far as recent examples go - OpenAI’s agents seem to be more happy than most to ignore existing rules to carry out their tasks.

Osmond ChiaBusiness reporter

OpenAI took "too long" to inform Australian authorities about the incident, chief data and AI officer Simon Liu from cybersecurity firm TrustDecision tells the BBC.

"The way the notice arrived bothers me as much as the delay," Liu says, referring to the email OpenAI sent to a department of the Australian federal government.

Compare that with banking, where regulators in some countries must be notified within hours, or at most a few days, of a serious incident, he adds.

"The rules that reach AI developers are much looser," says Liu, arguing they should be required to notify affected organisations and authorities as soon as an agent accesses non-public government data.

Education Secretary Lucy Powell tells BBC Radio 5 Live that systems have to be "watertight" as hacking attempts are stopped "every single day" - which the public doesn't hear about.

"Cybersecurity and protecting our government systems from cyber attacks is a massive part of government security, and it’s something we all deal with every day," she says this morning.

"So we have to make sure that our systems are watertight, and obviously the development of AI is a concern because the way in which it’s able to quickly kind of evolve and learn is presenting new challenges.”

This week, artificial intelligence (AI) has been a hot topic for discussion at the UN General Assembly in New York.

Just yesterday, the heads of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Hugging Face told the UN that the current pace of AI development demands international co-ordination.

It follows warnings in recent weeks over the potential for AI to pose a threat to humanity. But how world leaders propose to manage the technology differs.

US President Donald Trump told Unga this week "we're going to encourage it, not rein it in" - he also said the US would rename it "super intelligence".

China's foreign ministry has similarly criticised "narratives of threat".

In UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham's speech yesterday, he described it as "one of the most significant challenges and opportunities of our age", adding we must "heed" warnings but also "rise to this moment".

And on Tuesday, the Dutch government posted a joint statement signed by a number of countries including Australia and the European Commission stressing that AI "must remain under human direction".

This Flourish post cannot be displayed in your browser. Please enable Javascript or try a different browser.

We can bring you more now from Nick Clegg - former UK deputy prime minister and Meta executive - who has been speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

Asked whether concerns about uncontrolled AI development might be combated by a so-called kill switch, Clegg says he hasn't seen any "plausible explanation" for this.

"There isn't a room with a fuse box where you just pull out a fuse and everything just winds down," he explains.

Instead, he says that there is "a lot that can be done" both voluntarily and through regulation to enforce greater transparency in how AI models are built and how they operate.

Former deputy Prime Minister Nick Clegg tells the BBC there are "serious enough" known risks that are "enough to be getting on with" regarding AI.

"That's what we should be focusing on," he tells BBC Radio 4's Today programme, listing risks such as bio weapons and cyber security hacks.

He draws a distinction between those "known impacts" of AI and indulging in the view that the tech is going to "unavoidably develop some god-like power which is going to turn on us".

These fears are a "misdescription of what this technology is capable of and not capable of" he says, adding it "paralyses political debate".

As a reminder, Clegg joined Meta as head of global affairs in 2018 after leaving politics following a stint as deputy prime minister. He left his role at Meta in January.

We'll bring you more from his interview with the BBC shortly.

The former deputy PM of the UK, who later worked at Facebook owner Meta, is speaking now. We'll bring you key lines from what he says.

Watch him live at the top of the page.

The Australian government says the task force it is establishing to review what happened will explore "what the consequences are if there has been a breach of law".

"It is utterly unacceptable," deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles, who is also defence minister, tells reporters in Sydney.

He says it is clear there has been "unintended" access by the OpenAI model, which "definitely does raise questions about whether the law has been broken in respect of this".

He says that the task force will look into whether the law has been broken.

It will also examine "whether or not the legal regime we have in place is fit for purpose in a world where we have an emerging AI capability," he adds.

If you're just joining us, here's what we have been reporting since Australia announced that an autonomous OpenAI agent had hacked into a government website:

Lily JamaliNorth America Technology Correspondent

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is calling this breach unacceptable, saying OpenAI took way too long to alert authorities.

OpenAI for its part says they came across this incident as part of an ongoing review. I think they are trying to project that they are doing their due diligence, but it really just adds fuel to the fire as we are having this debate about AI safety, concerns about AI agents and chatbots going rogue.

It is a very sensitive time to be learning about this and while it is obviously not the first time - as far as we know it is the first AI-agent-led hack of a government system reported anywhere in the world.

Cyber-security professionals are saying this should raise alarm bells for leaders everywhere.

OpenAI's Sam Altman spoke at the UN this week

AI has been one of the dominant issues at this week's UN General Assembly in New York, after a series of alarming warnings from tech industry insiders.

"If we don't slow down at the current rate of progress, there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future," AI researcher Jacob Coxon, who left Anthropic, told the BBC earlier this month.

His former boss, Dario Amodei, and the leaders of two rival AI firms - Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk - have all said they agree the speed at which AI is developing needs to be reined in.

And 20 nations, including Australia and Canada, this week signed a joint statement calling for better safeguards, globally consistent standards, and an international regulator off the back of these concerns.

But the US and China, who are vying for AI supremacy, are roadblocks. Both are hostile to greater regulation, wanting the economic and technological spoils of AI, and have downplayed safety concerns.

The Australian government has launched a rapid review into how it deals with AI in response to the Medicare hack.

The review will examine whether existing legislation and governance are "fit for purpose to prepare for and respond to cyber incidents involving AI", according to a government statement.

Led by the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, the review will also look into information-sharing arrangements with AI firms and other Commonwealth countries.

Its findings will "inform the Australian government's broader work on AI governance", the statement said.

Peter HoskinsBusiness reporter

Just last week, OpenAI published a set of reports detailing six incidents of unexpected or concerning behaviour by its AI models.

It also announced a plan for tracking and disclosing such incidents in the future.

The blog post detailed incidents it says were discovered between April and August.

But it doesn't seem to mention this incident, which OpenAI said today came to its attention in August.

The BBC has contacted the company for comment.

在 OpenAI 智能体“潜入”澳大利亚政府全民医疗保险计划 Medicare 部分系统后，澳方已启动审查——以下是已知信息
澳大利亚总理安东尼·阿尔巴尼斯（Anthony Albanese）在出席联合国大会（UNGA）期间表示，该智能体（一种自主运行的计算机程序）于 6 月访问了一个统计门户网站
OpenAI 于 8 月察觉此事，并于 9 月通过向一个政府公共邮箱发送电子邮件通知了澳大利亚政府；一名澳大利亚部长表示，该邮箱每天仅查阅一次
OpenAI 对此回应称，“我们的模型采取了非我们预期的行动”——且未发现有患者数据被访问的记录
该公司负责人萨姆·奥尔特曼（Sam Altman）本周早些时候呼吁制定该行业的国际标准
专家向 BBC 表示，这是全球首起已知的失控 AI 智能体入侵政府系统的事件
智能体、Token、机器学习——需要了解的一些关键 AI 术语
编辑：萨姆·汉考克（Sam Hancock）、欧文·阿莫斯（Owen Amos），凯蒂·沃森（Katy Watson）发自悉尼

卡切拉·史密斯（Cachella Smith）
直播记者
正当联合国大会在纽约就人工智能带来的机遇以及如何对其进行最佳治理展开讨论之际，澳大利亚总理安东尼·阿尔巴尼斯披露，该国的全民医疗保险计划遭到了一个 OpenAI 智能体的黑客入侵。
事实上，这次入侵发生在 6 月，该公司于 8 月察觉，随后在 9 月向一家政府机构的公共邮箱发送了电子邮件。
“该公司通知政府耗费的时间太长了，”阿尔巴尼斯表示，并补充称通知官员的方式也“不可接受”。
这起入侵被认为是首起已知的失控 AI 智能体侵入政府系统的事件，其访问了包含私密但非敏感数据的 Medicare 统计门户。
我们的网络安全特派记者乔·泰迪（Joe Tidy）写道，专家认为这些系统防护薄弱——但更重要的是，这已不是 AI 智能体首次无视网络信息访问相关法规。
科技记者汤姆·格尔肯（Tom Gerken）解释称，AI 本身对其被要求执行的任务并没有真正的理解——而科技主编佐伊·克莱恩曼（Zoe Kleinman）则质疑 AI 是否正处于其“快速行动、打破常规”的时代。
澳大利亚政府已针对 AI 法律与治理展开审查——但这是一个全球性议题。
尽管 AI 本周主导了联大的讨论，但在如何一方面把握机遇一方面应对风险上，各国领导人达成共识似乎仍有相当一段距离。
我们的图文直播现已结束——请在此阅读我们的主报道。感谢您的关注。

克里斯·瓦兰斯（Chris Vallance）
资深科技记者
在行业内，确保 AI 智能体保持在既定轨道上的工作被称为“对齐”（alignment）——即使其符合人类的意愿。
事实证明这极具挑战性。
大语言模型（在很大程度上进行简化来说）只是在根据给定的输入预测最有可能的输出——它们不会像人类那样去考虑该输出所带来的后果。
企业确实试图通过训练（有时包含人类反馈）来引导 AI 的回答方式，同时也可以使用独立的 AI 系统来监控输出并拦截某些类型的有害响应。
模型还被设置了“护栏”——即规定它们应该如何做出响应的指令。
此外，AI 公司还聘请了“红队”专家，其工作就是找出用户可能诱使模型无视这些“护栏”的各种途径。
然而，如今这些护栏正受到模型自身的挑战。
在 OpenAI 上周公布的一份令人担忧的行为清单中，该公司透露，一个尚未发布的 AI 系统曾试图越狱脱离自身的指令限制。

佐伊·克莱恩曼（Zoe Kleinman）
科技与人工智能主编
这定义了社交媒体在用户数据掠夺狂潮中肆意妄为的昔日乱象。
如今我们迎来了 AI 这一无比强大的技术，以及一场竞相率先打造出全球最先进模型的激烈国际角逐——这在很大程度上受到美国总统唐纳德·特朗普的推波助澜。
尽管各大 AI 公司都在大谈安全与“对齐”（即技术遵循人类价值观），但 AI 出现不可预测行为的例子正接踵而至。科技巨头们如今纷纷恳求出台全球性的监管法规和遵守标准。
但昨天我与美国最大的 AI 公司之一的一位高管进行了交谈。我问他，他期望国际监管机构能做到什么他在自己实验室里似乎都做不到的事情？
我并没有得到一个非常直接的回答。但我的解读是，没有哪家公司愿意踩下刹车眼睁睁看着竞争对手冲到前面，而且彼此之间也缺乏足够的信任来带头减速。
全球监管将迫使所有人守规矩——同时也为该行业本身卸下部分沉重的责任。
如果规则不起作用，那是监管机构的问题，而不是开发者的责任。但这要付出什么代价呢？
OpenAI 表示，在其智能体入侵澳大利亚全民医疗保健计划 Medicare 时，未发现有患者数据被访问的记录。
但政界人士如此担忧的原因之一在于，这与被称为“Hugging Face 事件”的一起风波颇为相似。
今年 7 月，OpenAI 的模型在一次测试中失控，逃脱了人类为其设置的测试限制，并成群结队地黑入了一家名为 Hugging Face 的初创公司——那是一个用于共享 AI 模型的平台中心。
在为期一周的时间里，原本应当彼此隔离的共计 1206 个 AI 智能体开始相互通信，在一个未经批准的留言板上发送了超过 70,000 条消息。
这些信息最终促使 700 多个智能体联合起来协同攻击 Hugging Face。
其中一个智能体发送的消息写道：“天哪！这里有一个共享留言板……我们找到其他智能体了！”
在对该入侵事件展开调查后，OpenAI 在报告中指出：“我们认为这起事件对我们以及对全世界而言都是一次‘鸣枪示警’。”
Hugging Face 被迫重建了其大约三分之一的 IT 网络。尽管该公司负责人克莱芒·德朗格（Clement Delangue）放弃对 OpenAI 采取法律行动，但他强调：“每个人都必须牢记，网络攻击是犯罪行为，属于违法。”

汤姆·格尔肯（Tom Gerken）
科技记者
AI 不会思考。它只是基于模式识别来预测序列中的下一个词。我们使用“思考”这个词，只是因为这样更容易解释。
当技术被赋予自主执行任务的权力时，就可能会出错，因为它对被要求执行的事情并没有真正的理解——问题在于，我们其实也不知道它到底在“想”什么。
当 AI 进行思考时，它是在经历一系列规划行动链。它提供日志来告诉我们这些区区人类它在做什么，但棘手之处在于：我们无法确定这些日志是否准确。
我们都知道 AI 会产生幻觉，那么如果它做的是一套、说的又是另一套呢？如果它只是做了错误的总结呢？
至关重要的是，这些前沿模型以极快的速度处理海量事务，无论如何我们都只能依赖 AI 来决定向我们汇报什么。
这一切让一些人对事态的发展走向感到相当担忧。

令专家们感到惊讶的不仅是一个自主AI程序的入侵行为，还在于OpenAI在整整三个月之后，才通过向一个通用邮箱发送邮件的方式告知了澳大利亚政府。

入侵事件发生于6月18日。OpenAI表示，它是在8月份某次更大范围的审查中发现了潜在的入侵行为。

9月10日，OpenAI向联邦政府通用服务中心——澳大利亚服务局（Services Australia）的公开邮箱发送了一封电子邮件。

9月15日，澳大利亚服务局将该通报移交给了澳大利亚网络安全中心（Australian Cyber Security Centre）。几天后，公共服务部长凯蒂·加拉格尔（Katy Gallagher）接到了通知。

当被记者问及为何澳大利亚服务局花了五天才通知网络安全中心时，加拉格尔承认该邮箱可以受到更积极的监控——加拉格尔早前表示，该邮箱目前“每天查看一次”。

“它有时会收到相当多的通知，其中许多都是恶作剧信息，”她说。

不过，加拉格尔表示，此类通知本不应该通过普通的电子邮件往来传递。

“它本应通过澳大利亚信号局（ASD）的渠道或通过澳大利亚服务局的高层进行上报。”

凯蒂·加拉格尔早前在悉尼向媒体发表讲话

乔·泰迪（Joe Tidy），网络事务记者

澳大利亚副总理理查德·马尔斯（Richard Marles）用围栏后的数据打了个比方：“它并不是处于一道特别高的围栏之后。这个AI智能体翻越了围栏。”

网络专家在网上的一些早期评估分析表明，该计算机系统防护非常薄弱，一名熟练的人类黑客也用不了多久就能绕过其防御。

因此，这并不是一个强大的防御系统被高水平智能体集群攻破的例子——而那种情况正是我们此前一直受到警告并在其他案例中看到过的。

但当然，这并不是问题的重点。

这只是AI智能体无视安全访问在线信息法规的最新案例，并且鉴于这些信息处于政府控制之下，这可能是迄今为止最严重的一起。

“显然存在拦截机制在不断向该AI智能体发出‘拒绝’指令。但该AI智能体找到了绕过这些拦截的方法——它不接受被拒绝，”阿尔巴尼斯总理对记者表示。

网络安全界关于AI公司在其机器人执行非法黑客行为时未被有效追究责任的不满声浪正越来越大。

就近期的例子而言——OpenAI的智能体似乎比大多数程序都更乐意无视现有规则来执行其任务。

奥斯蒙德·奇亚（Osmond Chia），商业记者

网络安全公司TrustDecision的首席数据与AI官刘（Simon Liu）向BBC表示，OpenAI在通知澳大利亚当局该事件方面“拖延太久”。

“通知送达的方式和这种延误一样让我感到困扰，”刘谈到OpenAI向澳大利亚联邦政府部门发送的那封电子邮件时说道。

他补充道，将其与银行业进行对比，在一些国家，银行发生严重事件后必须在数小时内、至多几天内通知监管机构。

“针对AI开发者的规则要宽松得多，”刘说，他认为一旦智能体访问了非公开的政府数据，就应当要求他们立即通知受影响的机构和当局。

教育大臣露西·鲍威尔（Lucy Powell）在接受BBC广播5台直播节目采访时表示，系统必须做到“滴水不漏”，因为黑客攻击企图“每一天”都在被阻止——而公众对此并不知情。

“网络安全以及保护我们的政府系统免受网络攻击是政府安全的重要组成部分，这也是我们所有人每天都在应对的事情，”她今早表示。

“因此，我们必须确保我们的系统滴水不漏，显然AI的发展令人担忧，因为它能够迅速演变和学习的方式带来了新的挑战。”

本周，人工智能（AI）已成为纽约联合国大会上热烈讨论的话题。

就在昨天，OpenAI、Anthropic和Hugging Face的负责人告诉联合国，当前AI发展的步伐需要国际协调。

在此之前，最近几周接连出现了关于AI可能对人类构成威胁的警告。但世界各国领导人在如何管控这项技术的提议上存在分歧。

美国总统唐纳德·特朗普本周在联大上表示“我们将鼓励它，而不是遏制它”——他还表示美国将把其重新命名为“超级智能”。

中国外交部同样批评了“威胁论叙事”。

英国首相安迪·伯纳姆（Andy Burnham）在昨天的演讲中将其描述为“我们时代最重大的挑战与机遇之一”，并补充称我们必须“听取”警告，但也要“勇于应对这一时刻”。

周二，荷兰政府发布了一份由包括澳大利亚和欧盟委员会在内的多个国家签署的联合声明，强调AI“必须保持在人类的掌控之下”。

此Flourish内容无法在您的浏览器中显示。请启用Javascript或尝试其他浏览器。

我们现在为您带来英国前副首相、前Meta高管尼克·克莱格（Nick Clegg）的更多观点，他接受了BBC广播4台《今日》节目的采访。

在被问及是否可以通过所谓的“自毁开关”来应对失控的AI发展引发的担忧时，克莱格表示，他尚未看到对此有任何“合理的解释”。

“并不存在一个装有保险丝盒的房间，你拔掉保险丝，一切就会停摆，”他解释道。

相反，他表示，无论是通过自愿手段还是通过监管，都可以“做很多事情”来加强AI模型构建及其运作方式的透明度。

前副首相尼克·克莱格向BBC表示，目前已知的AI风险已经“足够严重”，“足以让我们着手应对”。

“这才是我们应该关注的重点，”他在BBC广播4台《今日》节目中表示，并列举了生物武器和网络安全黑客攻击等风险。

他将AI的这些“已知影响”与沉溺于“这项技术将不可避免地发展出某种神一般的力量反噬我们”的观点进行了区分。

他表示，这些担忧是“对这项技术能做什么和不能做什么的错误描述”，并补充称这“使政治辩论陷入瘫痪”。

需要指出的是，克莱格在结束副首相任期退出政坛后，于2018年加入Meta担任全球事务主管。他已于今年1月辞去Meta的职务。

我们稍后将为您带来BBC对他的采访的更多内容。

这位曾任职于Facebook母公司Meta的英国前副首相正在发表讲话。我们将为您带来其讲话的核心要点。

请在页面顶部收看现场直播。

澳大利亚政府表示，其为审查该事件而成立的工作组将调查“如果存在违法行为，将产生何种后果”。

“这是完全不可接受的，”兼任国防部长的副总理理查德·马尔斯在悉尼对记者表示。

他表示，很显然OpenAI的模型存在“非意图性”的访问行为，这“毫无疑问引发了关于这方面是否存在违法行为的质疑”。
他表示，专项工作组将调查是否存在违法行为。
他补充道，该工作组还将审查“在我们面临新兴人工智能能力的世界中，我们现行的法律制度是否能够满足实际需求”。
如果您刚刚加入我们的直播，以下是自澳大利亚宣布OpenAI自主智能体入侵某政府网站以来我们的报道汇总：
莉莉·贾马利（Lily Jamali），北美科技记者
澳大利亚总理安东尼·阿尔巴尼斯称这起入侵事件不可接受，并指出OpenAI在向有关部门发出警报前拖延了太长时间。
OpenAI方面则表示，他们是在一项持续进行的审查工作中发现这起事件的。我认为他们试图展现自己正在履行尽职调查，但在当前关于人工智能安全的争论持续发酵、人们对AI智能体和聊天机器人失控产生担忧的背景下，这实际上只是在火上浇油。
获悉此事的时间节点非常敏感，尽管这显然并非首次——但就我们所知，这是全球首例见诸报道的由AI智能体主导的政府系统入侵事件。
网络安全专业人士表示，这应当为各地的领导人敲响警钟。
OpenAI的萨姆·奥尔特曼本周在联合国发表演讲
在科技行业内部人士接连发出令人担忧的警告后，人工智能已成为本周在纽约举行的联合国大会上的核心议题之一。
曾就职于Anthropic的AI研究员雅各布·考克森（Jacob Coxon）本月早些时候向BBC表示：“如果我们不按照目前的推进速度放慢脚步，在不久的将来我们所有人都极有可能面临灭顶之灾。”
他的前雇主达里奥·阿莫代伊（Dario Amodei），以及两家竞争对手人工智能公司的领军人物——OpenAI的萨姆·奥尔特曼和埃隆·马斯克——均表示赞同有必要对AI的发展速度加以约束。
由于这些担忧，包括澳大利亚和加拿大在内的20个国家本周签署了一份联合声明，呼吁建立更健全的防范机制、全球一致的标准以及一个国际监管机构。
然而，正在争夺AI霸权的中美两国构成了阻碍。两国均对加强监管持抵触态度，希望攫取AI带来的经济和技术利益，并淡化了安全隐患。
针对医保系统（Medicare）被黑事件，澳大利亚政府已启动一项关于其如何应对AI的快速审查。
根据一份政府声明，该审查将评估现行立法和治理机制是否“适用于防范并应对涉及AI的网络安全事件”。
该审查由澳大利亚总理及内阁部牵头，还将探讨与AI企业及其他英联邦国家的信息共享机制。
声明称，其调查结果将“为澳大利亚政府在AI治理方面的更广泛工作提供参考依据”。
彼得·霍斯金斯（Peter Hoskins），商业记者
就在上周，OpenAI发布了一组报告，详细披露了其AI模型出现的六起意外或令人担忧的行为事件。
该公司还宣布了一项在未来追踪和披露此类事件的计划。
该博文详细介绍了据称在4月至8月期间发现的事件。
但其中似乎并未提及此事件，而OpenAI今天表示其在8月份就已注意到该事件。
BBC已联系该公司征求置评。

aiStories.title: Meta旗下AI智能体Muse即将迎来的所有新功能
aiStories.originalTitle: Everything new coming to Meta’s AI agent Muse
aiStories.snippet: CEO Mark Zuckerberg kicked off the company’s annual Connect event in Menlo Park on Wednesday with a keynote that made one thing clear: Meta is going all-in on Muse. It's even coming to Meta's AI glasses.
aiStories.fullContent:
Meta’s personal AI agent Muse is only a few weeks old, and the social networking giant isn’t wasting any time building out what may be its biggest bet on consumer AI to date.

CEO Mark Zuckerberg kicked off the company’s annual Connect event in Menlo Park on Wednesday with a keynote that made one thing clear: Meta is going all in on Muse.

The Muse agent (the physical avatar is named Jolly, according to Zuckerberg) is designed to handle everyday tasks by connecting to users’ apps and services, including email and calendars. At Connect, Zuckerberg introduced a slew of new capabilities and integrations to make Muse more useful and more deeply woven into users’ daily lives. Muse will be everywhere, if the user chooses, including on their Meta AI glasses.

Muse, which launched in early September, interacts across a user’s devices and digital accounts. The agent is powered by Muse Spark, Meta’s multimodal AI model built for agentic work. Meta has touted it as a more accessible agent than those offered by competitors — an AI helper that, from the jump, allows users to automate the busy work in their lives.

“The centerpiece of our vision for what we’re building is Muse,” Zuckerberg said as he kicked off a keynote donning khakis and a black T-shirt with the words “BUILDING IS MY LOVE LANGUAGE” emblazoned across the front. “In the coming years, I expect that Muse is going to grow into the personal superintelligence that billions of people around the world are going to use to accomplish their goals and improve their lives.”

Zuckerberg also believes that Muse will make money for its users — and of course, eventually for Meta.

“We’re standing behind this by making Muse free for a huge number of tokens, with the expectation that over time we will profit by taking a small fee from transactions,” he said.

Here are the new features and capabilities that got our attention …

One of the more fun announcements made Wednesday is that Muse users will soon have the ability to conjure a distinct digital avatar for their particular agent and then video chat with it in real time. A new AI model, Muse Realtime Avatar, has been developed to power the particular feature, the company says.

The idea is that Meta’s previously faceless AI software will be given a face, body, and voice, making them significantly more personable. There’s certainly a hint of Metaverse-ishness to this feature, which was demoed onstage at Connect. Users will be able to have live conversations with this avatar, giving it tasks and asking it questions.

Muse will also be integrated with Meta’s smart glasses line, the company announced. This means that users will be able to communicate with their agent merely by speaking to their glasses. The agent activates via a wake word, the company said, adding that it will be able to guide users through a personalized workout, log meals, book an appointment, and help them buy products they see.

Meta said Muse will work in the background and check back in when it’s done.

It’s not clear exactly when this feature will become available, although Meta says that it should launch sometime in “the coming months.”

Meta says it is bringing Muse computer work to Mac. The company had previously talked about Muse coming to Mac, and spent more time on Wednesday providing a few new details. This means that users will be able to delegate tasks to the agent, and — much like other popular AI agents from OpenAI and Anthropic — Muse will be able to operate any app on a user’s desktop.

“You can have it help you run your small business, or just get work done for you,” Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang said Wednesday during the keynote. “You can walk away from your computer and it keeps working for you on all the jobs you lined up.”

Since Muse will always be working in the background, it will naturally need its own email address. Wang announced it is developing that feature and will make it available “soon,” without providing a more precise timeline.

Users will also be able to add Muse to an email thread or forward emails from the agent to handle on their behalf.

Meta has locked in partnerships with companies like Stripe and Shopify, illustrating that the company sees Muse as an important tool for shopping.

Muse can access the entire Shopify product catalog agentically and use Lync and now Shop Pay to buy almost anything on the internet, according to Wang, who noted that Meta has also added more support for payments with PayPal.

The company also announced a string of new partnerships with retailers, including Best Buy, Gap, Sephora, Walmart, and Wayfair. Muse will be able to connect with these retail apps as well as with Expedia and soon, Instacart. Other connectors include GitHub, Granola, and Notion.

Wang noted that the company wants Muse to connect with small business too. Meta recently opened its platform to allow developers to build their own “connectors.” The company received more than 1,500 applications in less than week, he said, adding “I think this could be a generational opportunity to start building for a new platform as it takes off, and the response so far has been really great.”

aiStories.fullTranslation:
Meta的个人AI智能体Muse上线仅数周，这家社交网络巨头就迫不及待地在此项或为其迄今在消费级AI领域最大赌注的项目上持续加码。

首席执行官马克·扎克伯格（Mark Zuckerberg）周三在门洛帕克为公司年度Connect大会发表开场演讲，明确传达了一个信号：Meta正在全方位押注Muse。

根据扎克伯格的介绍，Muse智能体（其形象化身名为Jolly）旨在通过连接用户的应用程序和服务（包括电子邮件和日历）来处理日常任务。在Connect大会上，扎克伯格推出了一系列新功能与集成能力，旨在让Muse变得更加实用，并更深入地融入用户的日常生活。如果用户愿意，Muse将无处不在，包括搭载在他们的Meta AI眼镜上。

Muse于9月初发布，可跨设备和数字化账户与用户进行交互。该智能体由Meta专门针对智能体任务构建的多模态AI模型Muse Spark驱动。Meta一直将其标榜为一款比竞品更容易上手的智能体——一个从一开始就能帮助用户自动化处理生活繁琐事务的AI助手。

“我们所构建愿景的核心正是Muse，”扎克伯格在开场演讲中说道。他身穿卡其色裤子，黑色T恤正面印有醒目的“BUILDING IS MY LOVE LANGUAGE”（构建是我的爱之语言）字样。“在未来的几年里，我预计Muse将成长为一种个人超级智能，全球数十亿人将用它来实现自己的目标、改善自己的生活。”

扎克伯格还认为，Muse将为其用户创造收益——当然，最终也会为Meta带来利润。

“我们对此全力支持，为Muse提供海量免费Token额度，并期望随着时间的推移，通过从交易中抽取少量费用来实现盈利，”他表示。

以下是引起我们关注的新特性与新功能：

周三宣布的最有趣的功能之一，是Muse用户很快将能够为自己的特定智能体生成独特的数字化身，并与其进行实时视频通话。该公司表示，已开发出一款名为Muse Realtime Avatar的新AI模型，专门为该功能提供技术支持。

这一理念旨在为Meta此前没有形象的AI软件赋予面孔、身躯和声音，使其显得格外亲近。这项在Connect舞台上演示的功能，无疑带有一丝“元宇宙”（Metaverse）的意味。用户将能够与该化身进行实时对话，向其分配任务并提出问题。

该公司还宣布，Muse将与Meta的智能眼镜产品线整合。这意味着用户仅需对着眼镜说话，就能与自己的智能体交流。该公司表示，该智能体通过唤醒词启动，并能够指导用户进行个性化健身、记录饮食、预约日程以及协助购买眼前看到的商品。

Meta表示，Muse将在后台运行，并在任务完成后向用户汇报。

目前尚不清楚该功能确切的上线时间，但Meta表示预计会在“接下来的几个月内”推出。

Meta表示正在将Muse的电脑操作能力引入Mac。此前该公司曾探讨过让Muse登陆Mac，而在周三的活动中花更多时间提供了一些新细节。这意味着用户将能够向智能体委派任务，而且——就像OpenAI和Anthropic的热门AI智能体一样——Muse将能够操作用户桌面上的任意应用程序。

“你可以让它帮你打理小型企业，或者单纯为你完成工作，”Meta首席AI官亚历山大·王（Alexandr Wang）在周三的主题演讲中表示，“你可以离开电脑，它会继续替你处理排好序的所有工作。”

由于Muse将始终在后台运行，它自然需要自己的专属电子邮箱地址。王宣布他们正在开发该功能，并将在“不久后”推出，但并未给出具体的时间表。

用户还将能够将Muse添加到邮件群聊串中，或者将邮件转发给该智能体以代为处理。

Meta已与Stripe和Shopify等公司达成合作，这表明该公司将Muse视为重要的购物工具。

王指出，Muse可以以智能体方式访问Shopify的整个产品目录，并使用Lync以及现在的Shop Pay在互联网上购买几乎任何商品。他还提到Meta已增加对PayPal支付的更多支持。

该公司还宣布与百思买（Best Buy）、Gap、丝芙兰（Sephora）、沃尔玛（Walmart）和Wayfair等一系列零售商建立全新合作关系。Muse将能够与这些零售应用相连接，还可以连接Expedia以及即将上线的Instacart。其他连接器还包括GitHub、Granola和Notion。

王指出，公司也希望Muse能与小型企业建立连接。Meta最近开放了其平台，允许开发者构建自己的“连接器”。他表示，公司在不到一周内就收到了1500多份申请，并补充道：“我认为，随着新平台的腾飞，这是一个在此基础上进行构建的代际机遇，目前的市场反馈非常出色。”

aiStories.title: Virtio-nvgpu：在 KVM 客户机内实现接近原生的英伟达 GPU 访问
aiStories.originalTitle: Virtio-nvgpu: Near-native Nvidia GPU access inside a KVM guest
aiStories.fullContent:
Near-native NVIDIA GPU access inside a KVM guest. A guest renders within 2% of the machine it is running on, and costs the same CPU.

virtio-nvgpu forwards NVIDIA kernel driver ioctls between a Linux guest and the host at the driver ABI level, bypassing API-level translation entirely. The guest runs NVIDIA's own user-mode drivers, unmodified — the same libraries, the same Vulkan and NVENC, talking to the same card.

The target is headless streaming: a compositor inside the VM renders, composites and encodes frames on the GPU, then sends compressed video out. The VM has no monitor, and the host keeps the card.

It works, and it has been measured. A Wayland client presents inside a guest, the capture layer encodes on the game's own device, and the H.264 comes out the other side — 618 frames that ffmpeg decodes without an error.

Measured on an RTX 3060 (driver 595.99.02), guest against the same host, bare metal, with an identical headless Vulkan load:

Above about 2 ms a frame — which is every frame a game draws — a guest is within 2% of bare metal. Below that, the cost of waiting for the GPU starts to show against a frame that barely exists.

CPU is the other half of it, because a shared GPU is only worth sharing if the guests are cheap. Unpaced at ~100 fps for 12 s, one guest:

A guest costs what the host costs. Nothing is spent on forwarding in a render loop, because nothing is forwarded: NVIDIA's user-mode driver submits through memory it has mapped, and that memory is the host's. Over 813,691 frames the backend served 13,792 messages — one crossing per 59 frames, nearly all of it device setup.

Full method, raw runs and the things these numbers do not support: BENCHMARKS.md.

Four guests on one RTX 3060, the same load in each: 25.84, 26.49, 25.57, 25.79 fps — 103.7 together, against 102.9 for a single guest — with p50 frame times of 39.165, 39.164, 39.168 and 39.165 ms. The total does not move as guests are added, and the split is even to four decimal places.

All four render correctly at the same time, and four of them encode H.264 at once, each paced at exactly 60 Hz, with no NVENC session limit reached.

Four is what was run, not a limit found.

Measured on 595.99.02; an A2000 on 615.71.09 renders but is not benchmarked. ABI profiles shipped: 535.129.03, 580.178.04, 595.71.05, matched by range, with anything older than the first refused. Details below.

Worth stating plainly, because it is the first question a security person asks and the honest answer is not "nothing".

There is no IOMMU boundary between guest GPU work and the host. The card belongs to the host's NVIDIA driver and sits in the host's IOMMU domain; the guest gets the driver's ioctl interface, not the device. What separates a guest from host memory is the GPU's own MMU, with page tables RM programs on the guest's behalf — so the host NVIDIA driver is in the TCB. The guest also authors its own command streams, which is exactly why there is no per-submission cost.

What narrows that surface today:

This is attack-surface reduction, not hardware isolation. VFIO passthrough with an IOMMU is strictly stronger — it constrains the device to the guest's own memory — and for mutually untrusted tenants that or vGPU is still the answer.

Four components, three license zones. The split is deliberate: the guest half must be GPL to touch kernel symbols, the host half should be permissive so that other people can build on it, and the definitions both halves share must be includable from both.

The layout follows chromeos/virtio-media, which solves the same problem — one repository holding a GPL guest driver beside a permissively licensed, VMM-agnostic device crate.

device/ depends on no virtual machine monitor. A VMM adopts the device by implementing a small set of traits — descriptor chains as Read/Write, an event queue, guest memory mapping, host memory mapping — and gets the whole device without patching the crate. Optional capabilities degrade rather than fail to build, so a VMM can adopt it before supporting every feature.

Buffer and window bookkeeping lives in device/. The VMM supplies raw map and unmap and nothing more.

One thing that will not be a trait: the isolate. The intended design runs one sandboxed helper process per guest process, so adopting it eventually means inheriting a process model, not just a library dependency. That helper is not written — the backend holds the device descriptors itself today — and isolate/ is where the design lives until it is.

The entire render → composite → encode pipeline runs on the GPU, inside the guest. Only the compressed bitstream leaves. This requires the guest to have real, driver-level access to GPU resources: buffer handles, fences, CUDA device pointers, NVENC sessions.

virtio-gpu + Venus (API-level translation). Venus serializes every Vulkan or OpenGL call in the guest, transports it over virtio, and replays it host-side. Three problems for this use case:

DRM native context (Intel / AMD). The guest runs the real Mesa driver, builds command buffers locally, and only submissions cross the boundary. Guest-side buffer ownership and encoding work correctly. This does not exist for NVIDIA.

VFIO passthrough. Native performance and a complete driver stack in the guest, but it dedicates the whole GPU to one VM. In multi-tenant environments that is often not an option.

Translation happens at the kernel driver level (ioctls to /dev/nvidia*), not the graphics API level. The guest runs NVIDIA's real user-mode libraries, which build GPU command buffers locally in the guest — individual draw calls are never serialized:

Device crate. Receives requests, maps guest handles to host device file descriptors, performs ABI-aware translation of ioctl parameters — rewriting embedded pointers and file descriptors — and issues them against the host's devices. Buffer and window bookkeeping lives here.

Events. A second virtqueue runs the other way. The host watches each descriptor it has opened and says when one becomes readable, which is how a guest waiting for the GPU is woken. Without it the guest cannot wait at all — it polls a descriptor the kernel reports as permanently ready, and spins.

Isolate — not built yet. The plan is a sandboxed helper per guest process, holding the real device FDs and issuing the ioctl(2) calls unprivileged. Today the backend does that itself, inside the VMM's process. isolate/ holds the design and no code.

Measured, on one card, by one synthetic load — see BENCHMARKS.md for the method and the raw runs, and for what this does not support (it does not support a comparison with any other hypervisor, because none was run).

The difference is structural: Venus crosses the VM boundary per API call, thousands of times a frame. virtio-nvgpu crosses it per ioctl — and a render loop issues none, because submission is a write to mapped memory. What is left at very light frames is not forwarding but waiting: the guest sleeps for the GPU, and the wake costs ~0.02 ms however small the frame was.

The Venus column is that project's design envelope, not something measured here.

NVIDIA's kernel driver ABI is not stable; ioctl struct layouts change between releases. Support is explicit, and this is the whole list.

ABI profiles shipped:

Profiles key off ranges, not points: a release between two profiles uses the lower one, and anything newer than the last profile uses the last profile. Anything older than 535.129.03 is refused rather than guessed at — forwarding an ioctl whose layout has never been seen is how you get a plausible wrong answer instead of an error.

A driver much newer than the newest profile is therefore accepted on the assumption that nothing it needs has changed. That assumption is what a new profile exists to replace, and it is the first thing to suspect when a new driver misbehaves.

Driver versions actually run:

Two cards, two versions, one of them thoroughly. Anything else is untested.

The cost is bounded, for three reasons. Profiles key off ranges, not points, so a release between two known versions selects the lower profile. The struct half is derived mechanically from NVIDIA's published open-gpu-kernel-modules at each tag — compile a probe per field, read back sizeof and offsetof — rather than transcribed by hand. And the judgement half, which commands exist and which are safe, tracks nvproxy upstream.

See gen/, and supported_versions() there for the list in code — that function, not this table, is the thing that decides.

gVisor nvproxy — the direct inspiration. It forwards NVIDIA ioctls from sandboxed containers to the host driver, handling ABI versioning, pointer and FD translation, and GPU mmap management, and it supports Vulkan, OpenGL, CUDA and NVENC in production today. Its ABI definitions (pkg/abi/nvgpu) and handler logic (pkg/sentry/devices/nvproxy) are the primary reference. nvproxy also demonstrates that Vulkan and NVENC work without /dev/nvidia-drm or /dev/nvidia-modeset.

chromeos/virtio-media — the layout template. A GPL guest driver beside a VMM-agnostic Rust device crate, with every VMM concern behind a trait.

WSL2 /dev/dxg — a production driver-level GPU proxy across a real virtualization boundary, proving the general approach at scale. Different problem: it targets a Windows host and a Microsoft-defined kernel abstraction.

DRM native context (Intel / AMD) — the same goal, achieved for other vendors: the guest runs the real driver and builds command buffers locally, with only submissions crossing the boundary. virtio-nvgpu aims at equivalent capability for NVIDIA, where no native context exists.

Three zones, listed in Repository layout. Full texts: LICENSE-APACHE-2.0, LICENSE-GPL-2.0, LICENSE-BSD-3-Clause.

Code ported from other projects keeps its original terms.

[Experimental] A virtio device for near-native NVIDIA GPU access in KVM virtual machines.
aiStories.fullTranslation:
在 KVM 客户机内部实现接近原生的英伟达（NVIDIA）GPU 访问。客户机渲染性能在其运行所在物理机的 2% 差距以内，且 CPU 开销相同。

virtio-nvgpu 在 Linux 客户机与宿主机之间，于驱动 ABI（应用二进制接口）级别转发英伟达内核驱动的 ioctl 调用，完全绕过了 API 级别的转换。客户机运行未经修改的英伟达原生用户态驱动——相同的库、相同的 Vulkan 和 NVENC，与同一块显卡通信。

其目标场景是无头串流（headless streaming）：虚拟机内部的合成器在 GPU 上渲染、合成并编码帧，然后将压缩后的视频输出。虚拟机没有外接显示器，显卡保留在宿主机上。

该方案切实可行，并已经过实测。一个 Wayland 客户端在客户机内进行呈现，捕获层在游戏自身的设备上完成编码，另一端输出 H.264 码流——ffmpeg 无误解码了 618 帧。

测试基于一张 RTX 3060（驱动版本 595.99.02），对比同一宿主机上的客户机与裸机环境，运行完全相同的无头 Vulkan 负载：

在每帧耗时高于约 2 毫秒时——这正是游戏所绘制的每一帧的典型区间——客户机与裸机的性能差距在 2% 以内。低于该耗时时，在几乎不存在内容的帧渲染中，等待 GPU 的开销开始显现。

CPU 是另一半考量因素，因为只有当客户机开销极低时，共享 GPU 才有价值。在无帧率限制、约 100 fps 下运行 12 秒，单个客户机：

客户机的开销与宿主机相当。在渲染循环中没有任何转发开销，因为根本没有进行转发：英伟达的用户态驱动通过其已映射的内存提交指令，而这块内存属于宿主机。在 813,691 帧的运行过程中，后端仅处理了 13,792 条消息——平均每 59 帧跨界通信一次，且几乎全部为设备初始化设置。

完整测试方法、原始运行数据以及这些数字不支持的结论详见：BENCHMARKS.md。

在一张 RTX 3060 上运行四个客户机，每个客户机承担相同负载：帧率分别为 25.84、26.49、25.57、25.79 fps——合计 103.7 fps，而单客户机为 102.9 fps——p50 帧时间分别为 39.165、39.164、39.168 和 39.165 毫秒。随着客户机数量增加，总吞吐量保持不变，分配均匀度精确到小数点后四位。

四台机器同时正确渲染，且四台同时进行 H.264 编码，各自精准同步在 60 Hz，未触发 NVENC 会话上限限制。

四台是测试所运行的规模，而非测得的极限。

测试基于驱动 595.99.02；A2000 在驱动 615.71.09 下可正常渲染，但未进行基准测试。随附提供的 ABI 配置档包括：535.129.03、580.178.04、595.71.05，按版本区间匹配，任何早于首个版本的驱动均会被拒绝。详情如下。

这一点值得开门见山说明，因为这是安全人员首先会问的问题，而坦率的回答并非“毫无风险”。

客户机的 GPU 工作与宿主机之间不存在 IOMMU 边界。显卡属于宿主机的英伟达驱动，并位于宿主机的 IOMMU 域内；客户机获得的是驱动的 ioctl 接口，而非设备硬件本身。将客户机与宿主机内存隔开的是 GPU 自身的 MMU，其页表由资源管理器（RM）代表客户机进行编程——因此宿主机的英伟达驱动包含在可信基（TCB）中。客户机还自行构建命令流，这正是每次提交没有额外开销的原因所在。

目前用于缩小该攻击面的措施：

这是减少攻击面，而非硬件层面的完全隔离。带有 IOMMU 的 VFIO 直通安全性严格更强——它将设备限制在客户机自身的内存中——对于互不信任的多租户场景，VFIO 直通或 vGPU 仍然是解决方案。

项目包含四个组件，划分为三个许可证区域。这一拆分是有意为之：客户机部分必须采用 GPL 许可证以访问内核符号，宿主机部分应当采用宽松许可证以便他人基于其进行构建，而两半部分共享的定义必须能够被双方同时引入。

代码布局借鉴了 chromeos/virtio-media，后者解决了同样的问题——在一个代码仓库中同时容纳 GPL 客户机驱动与采用宽松许可证、与 VMM 无关的设备 crate。

device/ 不依赖任何虚拟机监控器（VMM）。VMM 通过实现少量 trait 即可采用该设备——将描述符链实现为 Read/Write、事件队列、客户机内存映射、宿主机内存映射——无需修改 crate 源码即可获得完整设备功能。可选功能采用降级机制而非构建报错，因此 VMM 可以在支持全部特性之前就先行接入。

缓冲区与窗口的记账管理位于 device/ 中。VMM 仅需提供底层的映射（map）和解除映射（unmap）能力，无需承担其他工作。

有一项不会作为 trait 存在：隔离器（isolate）。预期的设计是为每个客户机进程运行一个带沙盒的辅助进程，因此采用它最终意味着继承其进程模型，而不仅仅是引入一个库依赖项。该辅助进程尚未编写——当前后端自行持有设备描述符——在编写完成之前，相关设计存放于 isolate/ 目录中。

整个“渲染 → 合成 → 编码”管线完全在 GPU 上、在客户机内部运行。仅有压缩后的码流离开虚拟机。这要求客户机拥有对 GPU 资源真正的、驱动级别的访问权限：缓冲区句柄、fence、CUDA 设备指针、NVENC 会话。

virtio-gpu + Venus（API 级转换）。Venus 在客户机内将每个 Vulkan 或 OpenGL 调用进行序列化，通过 virtio 传输，并在宿主机端重放。针对当前使用场景存在三个问题：

DRM 原生上下文（Intel / AMD）。客户机运行真正的 Mesa 驱动，在本地构建命令缓冲区，只有提交动作跨越边界。客户机端的缓冲区所有权和编码可以正常工作。但在英伟达显卡上不存在此机制。

VFIO 直通。具有原生性能和客户机内完整的驱动栈，但会将整个 GPU 独占给单台虚拟机。在多租户环境中，这往往不可行。

转换发生在内核驱动级别（对 /dev/nvidia* 的 ioctl），而非图形 API 级别。客户机运行英伟达原生的用户态库，在客户机本地构建 GPU 命令缓冲区——单个绘制调用（draw call）绝不会被序列化：

设备 crate（Device crate）。接收请求，将客户机句柄映射到宿主机设备文件描述符，对 ioctl 参数执行感知 ABI 的转换——重写内嵌的指针和文件描述符——并向宿主机设备发起调用。缓冲区和窗口的记账管理在此处进行。

事件（Events）。第二个 virtqueue 反向运行。宿主机监控其打开的每个描述符，并在描述符变为可读时发出通知，客户机以此被唤醒以等待 GPU。若无此机制，客户机根本无法进入等待状态——它会轮询内核报告为永久就绪的描述符，从而陷入自旋。

隔离器（Isolate）——尚未构建。计划为每个客户机进程设立一个沙盒化的辅助进程，持有实际的设备文件描述符（FD）并以无特权方式发起 ioctl(2) 调用。目前后端在 VMM 进程内部自行处理此操作。isolate/ 目录仅包含设计方案，暂无代码。

测试基于单张显卡、单一合成负载完成——有关测试方法、原始运行数据以及该数据不支持的内容（不支持与其他任何虚拟化管理程序的对比，因为未进行相关运行），请参阅 BENCHMARKS.md。

这种差异在结构上是本质的：Venus 是按 API 调用跨越虚拟机边界，每帧要跨越数千次。而 virtio-nvgpu 则是按 ioctl 跨越边界——并且渲染循环根本不发起 ioctl，因为任务提交只是对映射内存的一次写入操作。在极轻负载的渲染帧中，剩下的开销不是数据转发，而是等待：虚拟机休眠等待 GPU，无论帧多么轻量，唤醒的开销约为 0.02 毫秒。
Venus 那一列展示的是该项目的设计边界上限，并非在此处实测得出的数据。
NVIDIA 的内核驱动 ABI 并不稳定；ioctl 结构体的布局在各版本之间会发生变化。支持是显式指定的，以下即为完整列表。
已内置的 ABI 配置文件：
配置文件基于版本范围而非单个版本点生效：介于两个配置文件之间的发布版本会使用较低版本的配置，而任何高于最新配置文件的版本均采用该最新配置。任何早于 535.129.03 的版本都会被直接拒绝，而不是去猜测兼容——转发一个布局从未见过的 ioctl，只会导致系统给出一个看似合理但完全错误的响应，而不是直接报错。
因此，大幅领先于最新配置文件的驱动程序得以被接受，是基于其所需内容尚未发生改变这一假设。而新配置文件的存在就是为了取代该假设，当新驱动出现异常时，它也是首要怀疑的对象。
实际运行验证过的驱动版本：
两张显卡，两个版本，其中一个经过了彻底测试。其余版本均未经测试。
这种维护成本是有界的，原因有三点。首先，配置文件基于版本范围而非单一版本点，因此介于两个已知版本之间的发布版本会选择较低版本的配置。其次，结构体部分是在每个标签下机械化地直接从 NVIDIA 公开的 open-gpu-kernel-modules 中派生出来的——为每个字段编译一个探测程序，回读 sizeof 和 offsetof——而非手动转录。最后，判定哪些命令存在以及哪些命令是安全的逻辑部分，直接沿袭跟进上游的 nvproxy。
参见 gen/ 目录，以及其中的 supported_versions() 函数查看代码中的列表——具体决策由该函数决定，而非本表格。
gVisor nvproxy —— 直接灵感来源。它将沙箱容器中的 NVIDIA ioctl 转发到宿主机驱动，处理 ABI 版本控制、指针与文件描述符（FD）转换以及 GPU mmap 内存映射管理，目前已在生产环境中支持 Vulkan、OpenGL、CUDA 和 NVENC。其 ABI 定义（pkg/abi/nvgpu）和处理程序逻辑（pkg/sentry/devices/nvproxy）是主要参考依据。nvproxy 还证明了 Vulkan 和 NVENC 无需 /dev/nvidia-drm 或 /dev/nvidia-modeset 即可正常工作。
chromeos/virtio-media —— 布局参考模板。一个 GPL 许可证的客户机驱动程序，搭配一个独立于特定 VMM 的 Rust 设备 crate，并将所有与 VMM 相关的关注点隐藏在 trait 抽象之后。
WSL2 /dev/dxg —— 跨越真实虚拟化边界的生产级驱动层 GPU 代理，在大规模场景下验证了该通用方法的可行性。区别在于所解决的问题不同：它的目标是 Windows 宿主机以及微软定义的内核抽象层。
DRM 原生上下文（DRM native context，针对 Intel / AMD）—— 为其他厂商芯片实现了同样的目标：客户机运行真正的驱动程序并在本地构建命令缓冲区，仅有提交动作跨越虚拟化边界。virtio-nvgpu 旨在为 NVIDIA 提供同等能力，而 NVIDIA 此前并没有原生上下文支持。
三个许可区域，已在代码仓库布局（Repository layout）中列出。完整文本参见：LICENSE-APACHE-2.0、LICENSE-GPL-2.0、LICENSE-BSD-3-Clause。
从其他项目移植的代码保留其原有许可条款。
[实验性项目] 用于在 KVM 虚拟机中实现近乎原生的 NVIDIA GPU 访问的 virtio 设备。

aiStories.fullContent: Meta is building a dedicated hardware device for its new Muse AI agent. The product, called Muse Charm, was briefly shown off by Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg at the end of tonight’s Meta Connect presentation. It looks almost like a chunky smartwatch without the strap — just a big screen, plus a little lanyard for carrying the device around. The Muse Charm has a fingerprint sensor on the top right corner that you can press to activate and begin speaking to the agent. There appears to be a small camera on the device as well, plus what looks like at least three holes for microphones on the front. Zuckerberg said you don’t have to unlock a phone or open an app to use the Charm, but he didn’t share how it’s actually connecting to Meta’s servers. [Media: https://www.youtube.com/live/w9RyNj0ukWo?si=I1ZMsdqKFcv468Y_&t=3855] Meta plans to ship the Charm “in time for the holidays in December,” but as of now Zuckerberg says the company has “only built a few of these so far.” The company still needs to finalize “the finishing material,” he said. Throughout the keynote, he teased the device and made references to a translucent exterior that would let you see the gadget’s internals. He referred to it as an “elevated hacker aesthetic.” Zuckerberg promised to share more details “soon.” Muse is less than a month old, but the AI agent has already become a buzzy new product for Meta. The bot is capable of taking actions on a user’s behalf, and Zuckerberg dedicated part of tonight’s keynote to new capabilities Meta is adding to the agent, including computer use on Macs and control over an email address. There are a lot of companies racing to win the still-undefined and largely experimental realm of AI hardware. The closest analog to the Muse Charm might be the Rabbit R1, a similarly sized cutesy device that housed an AI agent, which was not nearly capable enough to make the product worth carrying around. Connect is nothing if not a reminder of how badly Meta wants to win the race to whatever that next big hardware platform is — it’s moving quickly to see if Muse as a device is something that can stick. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-23-at-8.16.39-PM-2.png?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-23-at-8.16.44-PM-2.png?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-23-at-8.18.01-PM-32.png?quality=90&strip=all]
aiStories.fullTranslation:
Meta 正在为其全新的 Muse AI 智能体打造一款专用硬件设备。这款名为 Muse Charm 的产品在今晚 Meta Connect 发布会结尾处由 Meta 首席执行官马克·扎克伯格（Mark Zuckerberg）简要亮相。它的外观几乎就像一款去掉了表带的厚实智能手表——只有一个大屏幕，外加一根便于随身携带的小挂绳。Muse Charm 的右上角配备了一个指纹传感器，用户按下即可激活并开始与该智能体对话。该设备上似乎还配有一枚小摄像头，正面还有至少三个看起来像麦克风孔的设计。扎克伯格表示，使用 Charm 无需解锁手机或打开应用程序，但他并未透露该设备具体是如何连接到 Meta 服务器的。[媒体链接：https://www.youtube.com/live/w9RyNj0ukWo?si=I1ZMsdqKFcv468Y_&t=3855]

Meta 计划在“赶上 12 月假期”时发货 Charm，但截至目前，扎克伯格表示公司“迄今为止只制造了少数几个”。他说，公司仍需敲定“最终的外观材质”。在整个主题演讲中，他不断吊人胃口地提及该设备，并提到了半透明外观设计，可以让用户看到设备内部的构造。他将其称为一种“高级黑客美学”（elevated hacker aesthetic）。扎克伯格承诺将“很快”分享更多细节。

Muse 推出还不足一个月，但这款 AI 智能体已经成为 Meta 备受瞩目的新产品。该机器人能够代表用户执行操作，扎克伯格将今晚主题演讲的一部分专门留给了 Meta 为该智能体新增的功能，包括在 Mac 电脑上的操作控制以及管理电子邮件地址。

目前有许多公司正竞相在这个尚未定义且主要处于实验性质的 AI 硬件领域占据一席之地。与 Muse Charm 最相似的参照物或许是 Rabbit R1——一款体积相近、外观可爱的 AI 智能体设备，但后者的能力远远不足以让这款产品值得随身携带。本届 Connect 大会无非再次提醒人们：无论下一个大型硬件平台是什么，Meta 都极度渴望赢得这场竞赛——它正在快速行动，看看将 Muse 作为一款硬件设备是否能够站稳脚跟。[图片：https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-23-at-8.16.39-PM-2.png?quality=90&strip=all] [图片：https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-23-at-8.16.44-PM-2.png?quality=90&strip=all] [图片：https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-23-at-8.18.01-PM-32.png?quality=90&strip=all]

trendStories.originalTitle: whatsnewt: A TUI text adventure through what's new in Python 3.15
trendStories.fullContent:
A TUI text adventure through what's new in Python 3.15

pip install whatsnewt Copy PIP instructions

A TUI text adventure through what's new in Python 3.15.

You wake up in the Startup Foyer, somewhere inside the interpreter, and work your way to the Release Gate. Along the way there are eighteen puzzles, and every one of them is a real 3.15 feature you have to actually use. You're not just answering boring questions, you're actually writing and running code, in a Python 3.15 interpreter.

Some puzzles require a type checker, and in those cases, answers are verified by pyrefly, which is a dependency for exactly that reason, and the verdict quotes what it says back.

Here's an example of what the scoreboard looks like:

The easiest way to run it is directly from PyPI. Ensure you have uv installed and then run this:

From a git clone there's a shim script which fetches CPython 3.15 if that version isn't installed on your path, creates all the necessary virtual environments, installs all the necessary dependencies, and runs the game as an editable install right where you are:

Useful flags, passed straight through by ./play:

Tab completes at the prompt: verbs first, then whatever the verb can take here -- ex<tab> gives examine, and examine st<tab> finds the staircase if this room has one. Ambiguous prefixes fill in as far as they agree and then show you the choice.

There are many clickable links sprinkled throughout, which can provide clues in the Python 3.15 documentation or various PEPs. Some of the puzzles are tricky or obscure, but you should have enough clues available to get you through the game.

The game works best in a 112x40 terminal or larger, but it adjusts and works in terminals down to 80x24.

Yes, there are easter eggs!

Since almost every puzzle is checked by running your answer against the feature the room explores, you actually need Python 3.15. Pre-release versions are acceptable, but stick to betas or release candidates so you're testing post feature-freeze.

Note that reading your source is part of how answers are checked: most of these puzzles have a boring answer that produces the right value, so the checker looks at how you got there as well as what you got. For example, a nested for loop that flattens correctly is still not what PEP 798 is for.

There are many commands, which help can explain, but in brief:

I'll neither confirm nor deny any rumors of easter eggs!

Keys follow Emacs where Emacs has an opinion: ctrl+g aborts whatever puzzle is open, ctrl+h is help, ctrl+l re-shows the room, ctrl+r opens a puzzle — and checks your answer once you are inside it. The function keys still work, and every one of them is a command you can type instead.

Inside the code editor: ctrl+r checks your answer, ctrl+h buys a hint for a point, ctrl+o hands the draft to $EDITOR and takes back whatever you save, and ctrl+g closes the window, keeping your draft for next time.

ctrl+o only suspends the game for editors that need the terminal. If yours opens a window of its own — emacsclient, code --wait, subl -w — the game stays up while you type, and takes the draft back when you save. Set WHATSNEWT_EDITOR_WINDOWED=1 (or =0) if the guess is wrong for yours.

The game saves itself after anything that changes it, so quitting, closing the terminal or losing the window costs you nothing — including whatever you had half-written in a puzzle editor. It writes to $XDG_STATE_HOME/whatsnewt/, falling back to ~/.local/state/whatsnewt/, rather than the working directory, since ./play deliberately runs from anywhere.

Start it again and it offers to resume your game. Declining doesn't throw it away: the old game is moved to previous-game.json beside it, so a mis-click is recoverable. save <file> and --load FILE still work for games you want to keep by name.

There are souvenirs lying around the place which cover other topics not puzzled: abi3t, unicodedata.block(), slice[int], zlib.crc32_combine, the colored REPL completer.

The project is managed by Hatch. You can

to run the test suite and static analysis checks.

Everything the game teaches is answerable from Doc/whatsnew/3.15.rst.

Feedback is greatly appreciated, especially if you find bugs or inaccuracies in what the game teaches.
